passage:
Tuition note, Tuesday. Wasim (Class 4)
Wasim asked to do his maths worksheet in the side room where the TV plays cartoons for the little ones. He told me, "I can do both, ma'am. I'm fast." I let him try and kept an eye on him.
He looked up at every loud bit, laughed, then looked down and read the same sum again. Twenty sums took him fifty minutes; usually it's twenty-five. Six were wrong, mostly carrying mistakes he never makes. When I asked about the cartoon, he couldn't tell me how the episode ended.
Tomorrow I'll set a timer: sums first with the TV off, then ten minutes of cartoons as a treat. I'll write both times on the board so he can compare them himself.
Devika

qa.q: How long did the twenty sums take Wasim with the TV on?
qa.a: Twenty sums took him fifty minutes, when usually it's twenty-five.

qa.q: Why did Wasim believe he could do both?
qa.a: Wasim felt confident and quick, glancing back and forth, so it seemed he was doing both; he didn't notice rereading each sum or missing the end of the episode.

qa.q: What plan did Devika make, and how could it help Wasim see the difference?
qa.a: Sums first with the TV off, then cartoons as a treat; writing both times on the board lets Wasim compare with his own eyes.

qa.q: What would change if Devika simply banned the TV without the timer?
qa.a: Wasim might obey but still believe he could do both, because he would never see fifty minutes and twenty-five side by side.

grounding: It shows a boy who believes he can do sums and watch a cartoon together, while switching makes both slower and worse.

passage:
Saturday
Dear Diary,
Today I did my English homework AND watched the robot cartoon. Two things at once! Trisha didi said, "Little brother, you can't." But I did.
Okay, maybe not perfectly. I had to write ten sentences about my school. It took the whole cartoon and then more. Every time the robot yelled, I looked up and forgot my sentence. Didi checked it and found three words missing and "robot" written in sentence six. Ha. And I don't even know if the robot won.
Deepika from my class said she finished hers in fifteen minutes with no TV. Didi says tomorrow I'll try it her way and time it. I bet I'm still faster.
Kunal, age 9

qa.q: What word did Kunal write by mistake in sentence six?
qa.a: Kunal wrote "robot" in sentence six.

qa.q: Why does Kunal still think he'll be faster?
qa.a: Kunal feels proud and confident, because doing two things at once feels busy and quick, even though he kept forgetting sentences and missed the end of the cartoon. 😅

qa.q: What test could show Kunal whether the TV slows him down?
qa.a: Timing the ten sentences with no TV tomorrow and comparing, like Deepika's fifteen minutes, lets Kunal see the difference for himself.

qa.q: What might Trisha be thinking as she checks the homework?
qa.a: Trisha may find "robot" in the sentences funny but also want Kunal to notice the missing words, which is why she suggests a timed try.

grounding: It shows a boy who believes he did homework and a cartoon well together, while each switch made him slower and less accurate.

passage:
The power came back in the village that evening, and so did the cartoon channel on the old TV in the front room. Tejas, ten, spread his Hindi notebook on the floor right in front of it.
"I'll write and watch," he told his sister Vinita, who was sorting groundnuts. "My hand writes, my eyes watch. Easy."
By the time the buffalo came home, he had copied only half a page. Vinita looked over and pointed: two lines skipped, one word written twice. The cartoon had ended, and he could not tell her what had happened in it.
"So which one did you do?" she asked gently.
Tejas frowned at the page. The next evening he did his lesson on the back step first and saved the cartoon for after.

qa.q: How much had Tejas copied by the time the buffalo came home?
qa.a: He had copied only half a page, with two lines skipped and one word written twice.

qa.q: Why did "My hand writes, my eyes watch" feel reasonable to Tejas?
qa.a: Tejas felt confident and relaxed, believing hand and eyes could work separately; he did not notice his attention jumping back and forth.

qa.q: What choice did Tejas make the next evening, and why is it better?
qa.a: He did the lesson on the back step first and saved the cartoon for after, so each got his full attention in turn.

qa.q: How might Vinita's gentle question work differently from scolding?
qa.a: Asking "So which one did you do?" lets Tejas notice for himself that both suffered, so he is more likely to change than if he felt blamed.

grounding: It shows a village boy who believes he can copy his lesson and watch a cartoon together, while both come out worse.

passage: In their small flat in Buenos Aires, Diego, nine, spread his maths homework on the coffee table, right in front of the TV. His favourite cartoon, the one about the space dogs, was on. "I can do both," he told his sister Layla. "I'm fast." Layla, twelve, sat at the kitchen table with her own work and watched. Every time the space dogs barked, Diego's head came up. He'd watch for a minute, then look down and reread the question from the start. After forty minutes he had done six of the twenty sums. Two were wrong because he'd written 34 instead of 43. "Almost done," he said proudly. Layla looked at the clock. "Diego, I finished mine and read a chapter." Diego frowned at the page, then at the screen.

qa.q: How many of the twenty sums had Diego done after forty minutes?
qa.a: He had done six of the twenty sums.

qa.q: Why did Diego feel proud when he said "Almost done"?
qa.a: He believed he was handling both the cartoon and the maths well, without noticing how often he had to start questions again.

qa.q: What could Diego try tomorrow to finish faster?
qa.a: He could do the sums first with the TV off, then watch the cartoon as a reward, so he isn't rereading every question after each bark.

qa.q: What might Layla be thinking as she looks at the clock?
qa.a: Layla may feel a little smug but also puzzled that her brother can't see how much slower the cartoon is making him.

grounding: A boy doing maths with a cartoon on believes he is managing both, while switching makes him slower and less accurate.

passage: At the community centre's after-school club in Amritsar, the little ones watched cartoons on the big screen in one corner, and the older children did homework at long tables. Nilesh, eleven, dragged his chair until it faced the screen. "Ma'am, I can do both. English comprehension and cartoons. Easy." Gurleen, the volunteer teacher, let him try. She noticed his pencil stop every time the cartoon music changed. He answered question three twice and skipped question four. After an hour he had half a page, full of crossings-out. The next day Gurleen offered a deal: twenty minutes facing the wall, then ten minutes of cartoons. Nilesh grumbled. But in twenty minutes he finished the whole comprehension, neater than before. "That was weird," he said. "It felt slower, but it was faster."

qa.q: Which question did Nilesh answer twice?
qa.a: He answered question three twice.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel about doing homework and cartoons together, and how did that change?
qa.a: Nilesh felt confident it would be easy and grumbled at Gurleen's deal, but then felt surprised that twenty minutes facing the wall was faster, calling it "weird".

qa.q: What deal did Gurleen offer, and why did it work?
qa.a: Twenty minutes of homework facing the wall, then ten minutes of cartoons; with no switching, Nilesh finished the whole comprehension neatly.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel hearing Nilesh say it felt slower but was faster?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased that he discovered it for himself, which will stick better than any warning she could give 🙂

grounding: A boy sure he can do homework while watching cartoons works slower and messier until single-task time shows him the difference.
